passed.title: from_dicts only infers the schema from the first 100 dicts
passed.trap: `pl.from_dicts` scans at most `infer_schema_length=100` rows to infer the schema. A key that first appears after that window is not part of the inferred schema, so its column can silently go missing. A value whose type does not match the inferred dtype raises under the default `strict=True`. For heterogeneous records, pass `infer_schema_length=None` (a full scan) or declare an explicit `schema`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

rows = [{"a": i} for i in range(100)] + [{"a": 100, "b": "late"}]

df = pl.from_dicts(rows)
print(df.columns)

full = pl.from_dicts(rows, infer_schema_length=None)
print(full.columns)
print(full.tail(1))

passed.title: from_records treats square data as columns unless orient is given
passed.trap: When `orient=None`, `pl.from_records` guesses the orientation by matching the schema length against the data dimensions. If the guess is inconclusive, as with square data, it falls back to column orientation. A list of rows like `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]` with two column names is therefore silently transposed. Always pass `orient="row"` when your inner sequences are rows.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]

wrong = pl.from_records(data, schema=["a", "b"])
print(wrong)

right = pl.from_records(data, schema=["a", "b"], orient="row")
print(right)

passed.title: pl.repeat infers Int32 for integers and pl.ones defaults to Float64
passed.trap: With `dtype=None`, `pl.repeat` infers `Int32` for integer values unless `Int64` is needed to fit the value. It does not use the `Int64` you get from Python ints in a DataFrame. `pl.ones` defaults to `Float64` even though it holds whole numbers. These dtypes can cause schema mismatches when concatenating or comparing with `Int64` columns, so pass `dtype=` explicitly.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

print(pl.repeat(1, 3, eager=True).dtype)
print(pl.ones(3, eager=True).dtype)

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [10, 20, 30]})
print(df.schema)

out = df.with_columns(
    pl.repeat(1, pl.len(), dtype=pl.Int64).alias("one"),
    pl.ones(pl.len(), dtype=pl.Int64).alias("one_b"),
)
print(out.schema)
passed.output:
Int32
Float64
Schema({'x': Int64})
Schema({'x': Int64, 'one': Int64, 'one_b': Int64})

passed.title: pl.mean over several columns is per column, not a row-wise mean
passed.trap: `pl.mean("a", "b")` is sugar for `pl.col("a", "b").mean()`. It reduces each column vertically and returns one row with one mean per column. It does not average across columns like pandas `df.mean(axis=1)`. For a per-row mean, use `pl.mean_horizontal`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 6]})

# per-column means, one row
print(df.select(pl.mean("a", "b")))

# row-wise mean
print(df.with_columns(pl.mean_horizontal("a", "b").alias("row_mean")))

passed.title: pl.nth selects columns by position, not rows, and is strict
passed.trap: Unlike pandas `groupby(...).nth(n)`, which picks rows, `pl.nth` selects the n-th column(s) of the context. By default (`strict=True`) an out-of-bounds index raises. Pass `strict=False` to ignore indices that do not exist. To pick the n-th row of a column, use `Expr.get` (or `Expr.gather`) instead.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 8, 3], "b": [4, 5, 2]})

print(df.select(pl.nth(1)))  # column 'b', not row 1

try:
    df.select(pl.nth(0, 5))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)

print(df.select(pl.nth(0, 5, strict=False)))

# row at position 1 of column 'a'
print(df.select(pl.col("a").get(1)))

passed.title: pl.map_batches passes ONE list of Series to the function
passed.trap: The callable given to `pl.map_batches` receives a single argument: a sequence of Series, one per entry in `exprs`. It does not receive one positional argument per column, so `lambda a, b: a + b` fails. Index into the list instead, and set `return_dtype` so Polars does not need to infer it. Prefer native expressions such as `pl.sum_horizontal` when they exist.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [10, 20]})

try:
    df.select(pl.map_batches(["a", "b"], lambda a, b: a + b, return_dtype=pl.Int64))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)

out = df.select(
    pl.map_batches(["a", "b"], lambda s: s[0] + s[1], return_dtype=pl.Int64).alias("a_plus_b")
)
print(out)

print(df.select(pl.sum_horizontal("a", "b").alias("native")))

passed.title: json_normalize turns dicts past max_level into JSON strings
passed.trap: `pl.json_normalize` is unstable. Unlike pandas, it encodes any dictionary it does not unnest as JSON string data, never as objects. With `max_level` set, deeper dicts become `String` columns holding JSON text rather than nested values. Leave `max_level=None` to flatten every level, or decode the strings afterwards with `Expr.str.json_decode`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

data = [
    {"id": 1, "fitness": {"height": 180, "stats": {"bmi": 26}}},
    {"id": 2, "fitness": {"height": 155, "stats": {"bmi": 24}}},
]

shallow = pl.json_normalize(data, max_level=1)
print(shallow.schema)
print(shallow)

full = pl.json_normalize(data)
print(full.schema)
